items.prompt: What does the term "opportunity cost" mean?

options.label: The money price paid at the time of purchase
The value of the next-best alternative given up when making a choice
The extra revenue earned from selling one more unit
The total of all fixed costs a firm must pay

rubric: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone.
Distractors confuse it with money price, fixed cost or marginal revenue.

items.prompt: According to the law of demand, what happens to quantity demanded when the price of a good rises, other things equal?

options.label: It doubles
It falls
It stays the same
It rises

rubric: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
Distractors reverse or ignore the relationship.

items.prompt: What is the market equilibrium price?

options.label: The price set by the government as a legal maximum
The price at which buyers get the most possible surplus
The lowest price at which a firm can cover costs
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

rubric: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Distractors describe price ceilings, break-even or consumer surplus.

items.prompt: Which term describes a market with only one seller and no close substitutes?

options.label: Monopsony
Perfect competition
Oligopoly
Monopoly

rubric: A monopoly has a single seller.
Monopsony is a single buyer; oligopoly means few sellers.

items.prompt: What is a "fixed cost" for a firm?

options.label: A cost that rises with each unit produced
A cost that only occurs in the long run
A cost that does not change with the quantity produced
A cost that is fixed by the government

rubric: Fixed costs stay constant regardless of output in the short run.
Distractors confuse it with variable cost or regulation.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of externalities? Select all that apply.

options.label: A shopper paying a higher price after demand rises
A neighbour's garden that raises the value of surrounding homes
Factory pollution that harms nearby residents
A firm paying wages to its workers

rubric: Externalities are costs or benefits imposed on third parties outside a transaction.
Price changes and wages are market transactions, not externalities.

items.prompt: A student has one free evening. She can work a shift paying 80 dollars or attend a concert that costs 30 dollars. She chooses the concert. Which term names the 80 dollars she gives up in making this choice, as part of the cost of the concert?

options.label: Sunk cost
Marginal revenue
Opportunity cost
Fixed cost

rubric: Forgone wages are part of the opportunity cost.
Sunk cost is unrecoverable past spending, which does not apply here.

items.prompt: Why does a price ceiling set below the equilibrium price create a shortage?

options.label: Demand shifts left because buyers expect further price cuts
Supply shifts right because costs fall under the ceiling
Quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls at the lower price
Quantity supplied rises because producers earn more at the lower price

rubric: A below-equilibrium price raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied.
Distractors reverse movements or invent shifts.

items.prompt: Which event would shift the demand curve for coffee to the right?

options.label: A rise in consumers' incomes, if coffee is a normal good
A new technology that lowers coffee production costs
A rise in the price of coffee itself
A fall in the price of coffee beans used by growers

rubric: Higher income raises demand for normal goods, shifting demand right.
Input costs and technology shift supply; own price causes movement along the curve.

items.prompt: A good has a price elasticity of demand of 2.5. What does this tell you?

options.label: Price rises by 2.5 dollars when demand rises
Demand does not respond to price changes
Quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price does
Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price does

rubric: Elasticity above 1 means demand is elastic: quantity responds proportionally more.
Distractors describe inelastic demand or misread the number.

items.prompt: Why do firms in perfect competition act as price takers?

options.label: Each firm is so small and its product so identical that it cannot influence the market price
Each firm colludes with rivals to agree a common price
Each firm is large enough that the government sets its price
Each firm has a patent that fixes the price for buyers

rubric: Many small sellers of identical goods cannot affect price.
Distractors describe regulation, monopoly power or collusion.

items.prompt: Why is a public good such as national defence usually under-provided by private markets?

options.label: Consumers value it too little to ever want it
People cannot be excluded, so many will use it without paying
The good is too costly for any government to supply
Private firms are legally banned from supplying it

rubric: Non-excludability creates free riding, so private firms cannot collect payment.
Distractors invent cost, valuation or legal reasons.

items.prompt: Which changes would shift the supply curve of bread to the right? Select all that apply.

options.label: A rise in consumers' incomes
A rise in the price of bread
A new oven technology that cuts baking costs
A fall in the price of flour

rubric: Lower input costs and better technology raise supply at every price.
A higher bread price moves along the curve; income shifts demand.

items.prompt: A town's only bakery raises the price of its loaves from 4 to 5 dollars. Sales drop only slightly, from 100 to 96 loaves a day, because residents have few other places to buy bread. How should this demand be described?

options.label: Inelastic, because quantity falls proportionally less than price rises
Elastic, because quantity falls whenever price rises
Unit elastic, because both price and quantity changed
Perfectly elastic, because buyers can switch to other shops

rubric: A 25% price rise causing a 4% fall in quantity means inelastic demand.
Distractors treat any quantity fall as elastic or misread substitutes.

items.prompt: The price of coffee rises while everything else stays the same. Which describes the effect on the coffee market's demand?

options.label: A rightward shift of the whole supply curve for coffee
A movement up along the demand curve to a smaller quantity demanded
A leftward shift of the whole supply curve for coffee
A leftward shift of the whole demand curve for coffee

rubric: A change in a good's own price moves buyers along the demand curve; it does not shift the curve.
Shifting the curve confuses a change in quantity demanded with a change in demand.

items.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of tea rises, what happens in the coffee market?

options.label: Quantity demanded of coffee falls along its curve
Demand for coffee shifts left as buyers leave
Demand for coffee shifts right as buyers switch
Supply of coffee shifts right as sellers expand

rubric: A higher price of a substitute raises demand for the other good.
Treating tea and coffee as complements gives the leftward-shift distractor.

items.prompt: Demand for a product is described as elastic. What does that mean?

options.label: Quantity demanded changes by the same dollar amount as price
Quantity demanded does not change when the price changes
Quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price
Quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price

rubric: Elastic demand means the percentage change in quantity exceeds the percentage change in price.
The second option describes inelastic demand.

items.prompt: A bakery pays $2,000 monthly rent whether it bakes 100 loaves or 5,000 loaves. How is the rent classified?

options.label: An opportunity cost only, because it is not a cash cost
A fixed cost, because it does not vary with output
A marginal cost, because it is a cost of production
A variable cost, because it is paid every month

rubric: Costs that stay constant as output changes are fixed costs.
Paying regularly does not make a cost variable; variability depends on output.

items.prompt: A factory dumps waste into a river, harming downstream fishers who are not compensated. What does standard theory predict about the market for the factory's product?

options.label: Output is efficient, since fishers can sell fish instead
Too little is produced, since the harm lowers its sales
Too much is produced, since the factory ignores the harm
The efficient amount is produced, since prices adjust

rubric: A negative externality means private costs are below social costs, so output exceeds the efficient level.
Assuming prices automatically capture the harm ignores the missing market for pollution.

items.prompt: Which of the following would shift the supply curve for bicycles to the right? Select all that apply.

options.label: The price of aluminium used in frames falls
Consumer incomes rise and people want more bikes
The government pays producers a subsidy per bike
A new technology lowers the cost of making frames

rubric: Lower production costs and subsidies raise supply at every price.
Rising consumer income shifts demand, not supply.

items.prompt: A city caps apartment rents at $900, below the market-clearing rent of $1,200. Many landlords respond by converting units to other uses, while more people than before want to rent at the capped price. What does this situation illustrate?

options.label: A new equilibrium, since the cap lets the market clear at $900
A surplus, since landlords now offer more units than tenants want
A shift of demand right, since lower rents raise tenant incomes
A shortage, since quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at $900

rubric: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage because buyers want more than sellers supply at the capped price.
Calling it a surplus reverses the direction of the gap.

items.prompt: Demand is `Qd = 100 - 2P` and supply is `Qs = 20 + 3P`. What is the equilibrium price?
rubric: Other values come from algebra slips such as subtracting instead of adding terms.

items.prompt: A shop cuts its price from $10 to $8, and weekly sales rise from 100 to 130 units. By how much does weekly total revenue change?
rubric: Revenue goes from 10 x 100 = 1,000 to 8 x 130 = 1,040, a gain of $40.
Other answers come from looking only at the price drop or only at the quantity gain.

items.prompt: A firm's total cost is $500 at 10 units and $560 at 11 units. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
rubric: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit: 560 - 500 = 60.
$51 and $56 are average costs, which confuse average with marginal cost.

items.prompt: A firm sells each unit for $12 (so marginal revenue is $12). Its marginal costs for units 1 to 5 are $4, $6, $9, $11 and $15. To maximize profit, how many units should it produce?

options.label: 5 units
2 units
3 units
4 units

rubric: Produce each unit while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost; the 4th costs $11 < $12, the 5th costs $15 > $12.
Stopping early forgoes profitable units; going further adds units that lose money.

items.prompt: The price of a ticket rises 10% and the quantity bought falls 20%. What is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
rubric: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price: 20 / 10 = 2.
0.5 inverts the ratio.

items.prompt: In the market for pizza, which events would, taken alone, raise the equilibrium price? Assume pizza is a normal good. Select all that apply.

options.label: The price of cheese, a key input, rises sharply
Household incomes rise across the city
A health report turns many people off pizza
Most pizzerias adopt faster, cheaper ovens

rubric: Higher input costs cut supply and higher income raises demand for a normal good; both raise price.
Cheaper ovens raise supply and the report lowers demand, both lowering price.

items.prompt: A government sets a minimum price of $8 per bushel for wheat. The market-clearing price is $6. At $8, farmers want to sell 80 bushels and buyers want to buy 50 bushels. What happens in the market at the $8 floor?

options.label: A shortage of 30 bushels appears
A surplus of 30 bushels remains unsold
A surplus of 80 bushels remains unsold
A shortage of 50 bushels appears

rubric: A floor above equilibrium leaves quantity supplied (80) above quantity demanded (50), a surplus of 30.
Calling it a shortage mixes up a floor with a ceiling.

items.prompt: Demand for a product is `Qd = 100 - 2P` and supply is `Qs = 20 + 3P`. What is the equilibrium quantity?
rubric: Setting 100 - 2P = 20 + 3P gives P = 16, and Q = 100 - 32 = 68.
64 and 80 come from misreading the intercepts or stopping before substituting the price back into a curve.

items.prompt: A cafe raises the price of a sandwich from $10 to $12 and weekly sales fall from 120 to 80. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
rubric: Midpoint %ΔQ = 40/100 = 40% and %ΔP = 2/11 ≈ 18.2%, so elasticity ≈ 2.2.
1.67 results from using the starting quantity and price as the base instead of midpoints; 0.45 inverts the ratio.

items.prompt: A firm's total cost is `TC = 200 + 5q + q^2`. What is the marginal cost of producing the 11th unit?
rubric: TC(11) = 376 and TC(10) = 350, so the 11th unit adds 26.
25 is the derivative at q = 10, 34.2 is average total cost at 11, and 35 is average total cost at 10; none is the added cost of the 11th unit.

items.prompt: Demand is `Qd = 60 - P` and supply is `Qs = 2P`. The government imposes a $6 per-unit tax collected from sellers. What price do buyers pay after the tax?
rubric: Sellers receive Pb - 6, so 2(Pb - 6) = 60 - Pb gives Pb = 24.
26 assumes buyers bear the whole tax, 20 is the pre-tax price, and 22 splits the tax in half.

items.prompt: A perfectly competitive firm faces a market price of $30 and has marginal cost `MC = 2q + 10`. How many units should it produce to maximise profit?
rubric: Profit is maximised where P = MC: 30 = 2q + 10 gives q = 10.
15 divides price by the slope and ignores the intercept; 20 and 5 come from algebra slips.

items.prompt: In the market for wheat, which events shift the supply curve rather than cause a movement along it? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new seed technology lowers the cost of growing each tonne
The market price of wheat rises by 10%
Consumer incomes rise, so bread demand increases
A drought cuts yields across wheat-growing regions

rubric: Changes in production conditions such as weather and technology shift the supply curve.
A price change moves along the curve, and a change in income shifts demand, not supply.

items.prompt: A city transit agency estimates that the price elasticity of demand for bus rides is -0.4. It plans a 10% fare increase to raise revenue. Assume the estimate holds for this change. What should the agency predict about ridership and revenue?

options.label: Ridership falls about 25% and revenue falls because demand is elastic
Ridership falls about 4% and revenue falls because riders leave
Ridership falls 10% and revenue stays unchanged at current levels
Ridership falls about 4% and revenue rises about 5.6%

rubric: Quantity falls 0.4 x 10% = 4%, so revenue changes by about 1.10 x 0.96 - 1 = +5.6% because demand is inelastic.
The distractors treat demand as elastic or unit elastic, or assume any ridership loss cuts revenue.

items.prompt: After a gasoline price spike, consumption barely changes in the first month but is clearly lower after three years. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.label: Consumers' tastes drift away from driving whenever prices stay high for a long time
Gasoline turns into an inferior good as time passes, so people buy less of it
Supply of gasoline becomes perfectly inelastic over time, which forces consumption to fall
Demand is more elastic over the long run because drivers can change cars, homes and commutes

rubric: Adjustment costs limit short-run responses, while longer horizons allow substitution, making long-run demand more elastic.
The distractors invoke supply, inferior goods or tastes, none of which explains the time pattern in the price response.

items.prompt: A competitive firm's average total cost is $12 at its current output, and the price is $10. A manager says, "We lose money on every unit, so shut down now." Which step in this reasoning is faulty?

options.label: It overlooks that marginal revenue is below price, so the firm should produce where price equals ATC
It assumes price is set by the firm, when a competitive firm should raise price to cover its costs
It compares price with cost per unit, when only total revenue against total fixed cost should matter
It uses average total cost, ignoring that fixed costs are sunk and only average variable cost matters short-run

rubric: In the short run the firm should keep producing if price covers average variable cost, since fixed costs are paid either way.
The distractors misstate price-taking or marginal revenue, or swap the relevant cost comparison.

items.prompt: A monopolist and a competitive industry face the same demand and cost curves. Why does the monopolist choose a lower quantity?

options.label: Its marginal revenue lies below price because selling more requires cutting the price on all units
Its marginal cost is higher because a single firm cannot spread its fixed costs over output
It sets quantity where price equals marginal cost, but this point falls at a smaller output
It faces a flatter demand curve, so each extra unit sold brings in less revenue than before

rubric: A monopolist equates MR with MC, and MR is below price since the price cut applies to every unit sold.
The distractors invent cost or demand differences, or misstate the monopolist's rule as P = MC.

items.prompt: Two airlines on a route each earn high profits if both keep fares high. Each earns more by cutting fares when the other holds, yet both end up cutting and earning less. What best explains this outcome?

options.label: Cutting fares is each firm's dominant strategy, so the self-interested result is worse for both than cooperating
Government regulation forces fares down, which prevents the firms from reaching the joint-profit price
Fare cuts raise marginal cost, which pushes both airlines to a lower-profit equilibrium over time
Each airline misjudges demand elasticity, so a fare cut looks profitable although it is actually not

rubric: The payoffs form a prisoner's dilemma: undercutting is the best reply whatever the rival does, yet both do worse.
The distractors replace strategic interdependence with misjudgment, regulation or cost effects not in the situation.

items.prompt: A factory's production releases pollution that harms nearby residents, and the market output is higher than the socially best level. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: Residents' costs are included in price, but the factory's profits push output beyond the optimum
The private marginal cost the factory bears is below the social marginal cost, so it overproduces
The factory's marginal benefit curve lies above demand, so the market quantity overshoots
Social marginal cost is below private marginal cost, so the factory produces too much output

rubric: A negative externality leaves the external harm out of the factory's costs, so private MC is below social MC and output is too high.
Distractors reverse the cost relationship or wrongly say the harm is already priced.

items.prompt: Which features, taken together, are consistent with a market being a natural monopoly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Average total cost that keeps falling across the whole range of market demand
Many small firms that each earn profit while competing on price
Very large fixed costs compared with the marginal cost of serving a customer
Average total cost that starts rising at a small fraction of market demand

rubric: Large fixed costs and falling average cost over the full market range mean one firm serves demand most cheaply.
Rising cost at small output, or many profitable small firms, would show room for competition.

items.prompt: In a used-car market, buyers cannot tell good cars from bad ones, so they offer only the average value. Owners of good cars find the offer too low and withdraw them, so the average quality falls and offers drop again. What best diagnoses this problem?

options.label: Adverse selection from hidden quality, which drives out high-quality sellers and degrades the market
Moral hazard, because sellers change their behaviour after a sale since the buyer has taken on the risk
A negative externality, because low-quality cars impose uncompensated costs on third parties on the road
A binding price ceiling, because the offered price is held below the level where supply meets demand

rubric: Asymmetric information before the deal leads to adverse selection, the lemons problem.
Moral hazard concerns behaviour after a contract, and externalities and price ceilings do not describe the unravelling from hidden quality.

items.prompt: A per-unit tax is collected from sellers of a good, and buyers end up bearing most of it. Which feature of the market best explains this split?

options.label: Sellers are legally liable, so they raise price by the whole tax regardless of elasticity
Supply is less elastic than demand, so sellers cannot avoid the tax and pass it on to buyers
The tax shifts the demand curve left, so the price buyers pay falls by the full tax amount
Demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers cut purchases less than sellers cut output

rubric: The side with the less elastic curve bears more of the tax, and here that is demand.
Distractors reverse the elasticity rule or treat legal liability as economic incidence.

items.prompt: A firm raises its price by 10% and total revenue falls by 4%. Which diagnosis fits this evidence?

options.label: Demand is elastic over this range, because quantity fell by more than 10%
Demand is inelastic, because quantity fell by less than 10% over this price range
Demand is unit elastic, because revenue should be unchanged when price rises
Supply is elastic, because lower costs must have reduced the firm's revenue

rubric: Revenue falls after a price rise only if the percentage fall in quantity exceeds the percentage price rise, which means elastic demand.
Distractors confuse the revenue direction rule for inelastic and unit elastic demand.

items.prompt: A firm's average total cost fell when output rose from 100 to 101 units, even though its marginal cost was rising over that range. What must be true at that output?

options.label: Marginal cost equals average total cost, because the average is at its minimum point
Marginal cost is below average total cost, because a marginal unit under the average lowers it
Marginal cost is above average total cost, because rising marginal cost pulls the average up
Fixed costs fell, because average cost can only decline when total fixed cost drops

rubric: Average cost falls only when the marginal unit costs less than the current average, even if marginal cost is rising.
Distractors assume rising marginal cost must raise the average or that fixed cost must change.

items.prompt: A competitive firm faces a market price of 8. At its output, average total cost is 10 and average variable cost is 6. Why is operating in the short run still better than shutting down?

options.label: Average total cost is only slightly above price, so the loss is too small to matter
Fixed costs can be avoided by shutting down, but only after a full year of losses
Price covers average variable cost, so each unit contributes to fixed costs owed either way
Price exceeds marginal revenue, so each unit adds profit that offsets the overall loss

rubric: With fixed costs sunk in the short run, operating is better whenever price at least covers average variable cost.
Distractors misuse marginal revenue, treat the loss size as decisive, or deny that fixed costs are sunk.

items.prompt: In a competitive market for strawberries, both the equilibrium price and the quantity sold rise this season. Which change best accounts for this?

options.label: A movement down the demand curve, because a lower price encourages greater purchases
A rightward shift of supply, because more strawberries are offered so sales rise
A rightward shift of demand, because higher demand raises both price and quantity
A leftward shift of supply, because a lower supply pushes the price up and sales along with it

rubric: Only a demand increase raises price and quantity together, holding supply fixed.
Distractors give a supply shift or movement that would move price and quantity in opposite directions.

items.prompt: A binding price floor is set above the equilibrium price in a competitive market. Which outcomes follow? Select all that apply.

options.label: A shortage appears that pushes the market price up even further
Some mutually beneficial trades no longer occur, creating deadweight loss
Quantity traded rises above the original equilibrium quantity
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the floor price
Quantity actually traded is limited by buyers' demand at the floor

rubric: A floor above equilibrium creates a surplus, trade is set by the short side (demand), and lost trades cause deadweight loss.
Distractors confuse a floor with a ceiling by suggesting a shortage or higher trade.

items.prompt: A firm that sells a niche software license estimates that at its current price, the price elasticity of demand is -0.8. Each extra license sold has a small positive marginal cost. An analyst is asked whether the current price maximises profit. What should the analyst conclude?

options.label: Yes, because positive marginal cost means the firm is already at the right output
No, because marginal revenue is negative, so raising price would raise revenue and cut costs
No, because the firm should cut price, since this raises quantity and so revenue and profit
Yes, because inelastic demand shows that customers value the license and revenue is stable

rubric: With inelastic demand, marginal revenue is negative while marginal cost is positive, so a price rise raises profit.
Distractors treat inelastic demand as a sign of optimality or recommend a price cut that lowers revenue.

items.prompt: A regulator knows each unit of a factory's output imposes a constant external damage of 5, but does not know the factory's costs. The goal is the efficient output at least information cost. Which policy best meets this?

options.label: A quota fixed at last year's output, so damage cannot rise above its present level
A per-unit tax of 5, so the firm weighs the full social cost and picks output itself
A subsidy for each unit not produced, equal to the firm's private profit per unit
A ban on production, so the damage is eliminated for certain with no cost estimates

rubric: A tax equal to marginal external damage makes the firm internalise the externality and choose the efficient output.
Distractors fix an arbitrary quantity or eliminate output without balancing benefits against damage.

items.prompt: A cinema wants to raise profit with a student discount. Criteria: students must be more price-sensitive than other buyers, and discounted tickets must not be resold to non-students. Which design best meets both?

options.label: A discount for any group booking, because large groups buy more tickets overall
A discount only at the box office on presentation of student ID matching the ticket holder
A transferable discount voucher sold in bulk, so students can share it with friends
A discount on every ticket sold online, so the cinema reaches students quickly

rubric: ID-checked entry separates the more elastic group and blocks resale.
Distractors fail either the sorting criterion or the anti-resale criterion.

items.prompt: A commentator says: "A monopolist is inefficient because it earns profit by charging above cost." Which critique of this claim is strongest?

options.label: The claim is wrong, because monopolists normally price at marginal cost to avoid regulation
The claim is incomplete, because monopolies are inefficient only when average cost is not minimised
The claim is correct, because profit is the same thing as deadweight loss in a market
The inefficiency comes from price exceeding marginal cost, which cuts output below the level where marginal benefit equals marginal cost, not from profit

rubric: Deadweight loss arises from restricted output where price exceeds marginal cost, not from profit as such.
Distractors equate profit with deadweight loss or misstate monopoly pricing.

items.prompt: Two rival firms propose a merger that would raise the market HHI from 800 to 2,000. To judge whether prices are likely to rise, which additional evidence is most useful?

options.label: Combined profit last year, which shows whether both firms are financially healthy
Share price reaction on announcement, since investors know the future price path
How closely the firms' products substitute and how easily new rivals could enter the market
Headcount of the merged firm, since larger employers always set higher prices

rubric: Price effects depend on closeness of competition and entry conditions, not just concentration.
Distractors use financial or size indicators that do not measure market power.

items.prompt: Residents of a neighbourhood all benefit from street lighting, and no one can be excluded. Criteria: the provision level should be efficient and free-riding should not undersupply it. Which approach best meets these?

options.label: Voluntary donations, since residents who value light will give the efficient amount
Tax-funded provision at the level where the sum of residents' marginal benefits equals marginal cost
Per-user fees collected by a private firm, since users then pay for what they consume
Tax-funded provision at the level where the average resident's marginal benefit equals total cost

rubric: For a public good, efficiency requires summing marginal benefits across users and equating to marginal cost, with funding that avoids free-riding.
Distractors rely on donations, fees that cannot exclude, or a wrong efficiency rule.

items.prompt: A councillor argues: "Rent control makes tenants better off, so it is efficient." Which are valid critiques of this argument? Select all that apply.

options.label: Controlled units may go to tenants who do not value them most, wasting potential gains
Transfers to current tenants do not show efficiency, since trades that benefit both sides are lost
Landlords may supply fewer or lower-quality units over time, shrinking the rental market
Controls raise the market rent of regulated units, so tenants lose overall
Efficiency requires every tenant to pay the same rent, which control does not ensure

rubric: Valid critiques cover reduced supply and quality, misallocation, and the gap between a transfer and efficiency.
Distractors invent an equal-rent requirement or claim controlled rents rise.

items.prompt: A city wants to cut downtown rush-hour congestion. Criteria: the policy should charge drivers close to the delay cost they impose, targeted by time and place. The options are a higher national fuel tax, a flat annual car registration fee, a time-varying charge for entering the central zone, and free public transit. Which best meets the criteria?

options.label: Free public transit, because lower fares always empty the roads at peak times
A time-varying central zone charge, because it prices the delay cost where and when it arises
A higher fuel tax, because driving more costs more and so every trip becomes pricier
A flat annual registration fee, because owners will then decide whether to keep cars

rubric: A zone charge that varies with time targets the marginal congestion externality.
Distractors price driving everywhere or only ownership, which does not target peak downtown trips.

items.prompt: A legislature levies a $2 per-unit tax on sellers, arguing that sellers will therefore bear the whole burden. Which critique of that argument is best?

options.label: Sellers bear the whole tax whenever supply is elastic, because they can then shift output out of the taxed market
Buyers always bear the whole tax, because sellers can raise the price by the full amount of the tax in the long run
Incidence depends on relative elasticities of supply and demand, so the legal payer may bear far less than the whole tax
The burden splits equally whenever the tax is collected from sellers, because the market price rises by half the tax

rubric: Economic incidence depends on the relative elasticities, not on who remits the tax.
Distractors assume a fixed split or all-on-one-side outcome, which ignores elasticity.

items.prompt: A monopolist faces constant-elasticity demand with elasticity -2 and constant marginal cost c, and prices at the profit-maximising markup. A per-unit tax t is imposed. Which evaluation of the pass-through to price is correct?

options.label: Price rises by less than t, since a monopolist absorbs part of the tax to protect its sales volume
Price rises by t/2, since marginal revenue has twice the slope of the demand curve
Price rises by exactly t, since marginal cost rises by t and the dollar markup is unchanged
Price rises by 2t, more than the tax, since the markup multiplies marginal cost including the tax

rubric: With elasticity -2, price = 2 x marginal cost, so price becomes 2(c + t) and rises by 2t.
The t/2 distractor applies the linear-demand result, and the exactly-t distractor assumes a fixed dollar markup.

items.prompt: A regulator proposes making a factory liable for smoke that damages a neighbouring laundry, claiming this is needed to reach the efficient smoke level. Property rights are clear and bargaining costs are negligible. Which critique is best?

options.label: Giving the rights to the laundry would yield less smoke than is efficient, since the laundry will refuse any payment offer
Bargaining reaches the same efficient smoke level under either assignment, so the assignment mainly changes who pays whom
Efficiency requires liability on the factory, since a polluter without liability ignores damage and bargaining cannot fix that
Private bargaining fails with few parties, so the proposal is needed whichever way the rights are assigned

rubric: Under the Coase theorem with low transaction costs, the efficient outcome is independent of the initial rights assignment; distribution differs.
Distractors assume bargaining fails or that liability is needed for efficiency.

items.prompt: A seller with constant marginal cost splits customers into two groups with different demand and charges each group its own monopoly price instead of one price. Total output is the same as under a single price. What is the welfare effect?

options.label: Welfare rises if profit rises by more than consumer surplus falls, because the seller's gain is then the larger one
Welfare rises, because each group now pays a price that better matches its own willingness to pay
Welfare is unchanged, because the consumer surplus lost is exactly captured by the seller as extra profit
Welfare falls, because the same units go to some lower-value buyers while some higher-value buyers go without

rubric: With unchanged output, the only change is misallocation across groups, which lowers total surplus.
Distractors treat transfers between consumers and the seller as welfare gains.

items.prompt: A regulator must price a natural monopoly with falling average cost. Criteria: efficient usage at the margin, no taxpayer subsidy, and every served customer still willing to participate. Which scheme best meets all three?

options.label: Price at average cost, which breaks even and keeps marginal usage close to efficient for all customers
Price at marginal cost with no other charge, since efficient pricing ensures the firm covers its total cost
The unregulated monopoly price with a profit cap, which avoids subsidy and keeps marginal usage fully efficient
Marginal-cost price plus a fixed access fee covering the fixed cost, provided each customer's surplus exceeds the fee

rubric: A two-part tariff gives marginal-cost usage prices and recovers fixed cost through the fee, if participation holds.
Marginal-cost pricing alone leaves a loss under falling average cost; average-cost pricing distorts usage.

items.prompt: Which are valid criticisms of inferring a firm's market power from a high Herfindahl index alone? Select all that apply.

options.label: The index cannot be computed when any firm holds under 1 percent share
The index ignores demand elasticity, so a concentrated market with elastic demand may show small markups
Market definition may omit close substitutes, which overstates concentration
Squaring shares makes the index fall when the largest firm takes share from a small rival
Low entry barriers can discipline prices even in a market with few firms

rubric: Market definition, contestability and demand elasticity all affect market power beyond concentration.
The last two options are false: the index handles small firms, and it rises when a large firm gains share.

items.prompt: In an online used-car market, sellers know their car's quality but buyers do not, so buyers offer the average price and owners of good cars withdraw. The platform wants good cars to trade again, at low cost, without banning private sellers or fixing prices. Which measure best fits?

options.label: Offer seller-paid inspection with a limited warranty, which costs good-car owners less than lemon owners and so signals quality
Cap all listing prices at the market average so that buyers never risk overpaying for a poor car
Publish the average sale price daily so that buyers can compare offers and judge each car better
Require buyers to pay a premium into a pool so that average-price offers rise for every seller

rubric: A warranty or inspection is a credible signal because it is costlier for owners of low-quality cars.
Distractors leave information asymmetry in place or raise prices without separating good from bad cars.

items.prompt: A software firm serves high-value and low-value customers it cannot tell apart. Design one public price list that captures the most profit from both types.

options.label: Sell a single version at the low type's value, so all customers buy and no one gains by misreporting
Offer a basic and a premium version, pricing premium so high types prefer it over basic at the basic price
Sell a single version at the high type's value, which always maximises profit since each sale earns the largest margin
Ask each customer to declare a type and charge the matching monopoly price, so each pays exactly their value

rubric: A menu with incentive-compatible quality-differentiated versions lets types self-select and extracts more than one price.
Declaring types is not credible, since high types would claim to be low; single prices ignore the screening gain.

items.prompt: Demand is P = 100 - Q. Private marginal cost is 20 + Q, and each unit imposes external damage of 0.5Q. Design a per-unit tax that induces the efficient quantity. What tax should be set?
rubric: Social marginal cost 20 + 1.5Q meets demand at Q = 32, where external damage is 16, so the tax is 16.
$20 and $10 use the wrong quantity or damage; $40 is the unregulated quantity.

items.prompt: A seller of one indivisible item faces several risk-averse bidders with independent private values. Design the sale format that maximises expected revenue among these options.

options.label: Any standard format, since revenue equivalence holds regardless of how bidders feel about risk
First-price sealed-bid auction, since risk-averse bidders bid higher to avoid losing, which raises revenue over second-price
Second-price sealed-bid auction, since truthful bidding means the winner always pays their full value
Ascending English auction, since open bidding reveals information and pushes the price above the second-highest value

rubric: Revenue equivalence needs risk-neutral bidders; with risk aversion, first-price bids are higher and revenue is greater.
Distractors assume truthful bidding pays full value or that equivalence still holds.

items.prompt: A firm hires a risk-averse manager whose effort is unobservable and whose output is partly luck. Design a pay contract that balances incentives and insurance.

options.label: Fixed salary plus a share of output strictly between zero and one, set lower when output noise or risk aversion is higher
Sell the entire output to the manager for a fixed fee, giving the strongest incentive at no cost in risk
Fixed salary alone, since a risk-averse agent prefers certainty and effort then follows from the manager's conscientiousness
A bonus only if output beats the best past result, which gives the strongest incentive without imposing any risk

rubric: The optimal contract trades incentives against risk-bearing costs, so a partial output share is used.
Flat pay kills effort incentives; selling the firm loads all risk on a risk-averse agent.

items.prompt: A fishery has 50 vessels with differing costs. The design must cap total catch at the scientific limit, keep enforcement cheap, and have the fish landed by the lowest-cost vessels. Which design fits?

options.label: An equal non-transferable quota for each vessel, which caps the catch and gives every vessel the same share
A flat license fee for all vessels set high enough to cut total effort down to the cap
A total allowable catch split into individual quotas that vessels can trade with each other
An open season that ends when the cap is reached, so the fastest and cheapest vessels land the most fish

rubric: Tradable quotas cap the catch and let low-cost vessels buy quota from high-cost ones.
Non-transferable quotas freeze inefficient allocation; open seasons cause races that raise costs.

items.prompt: A city's flat $5 daily downtown charge barely cuts peak congestion. Constraints: cut peak traffic efficiently, leave low-income residents no worse off on average, and keep the incentive to drive less. Which changes meet them? Select all that apply.

options.label: Return revenue as equal lump-sum payments per resident, not tied to driving
Return revenue as rebates proportional to miles driven
Vary the charge by time so that peak periods cost more than off-peak periods
Set the peak charge near the marginal external cost of an added trip
Exempt all vehicles during the morning peak to protect commuters

rubric: Time-varying pricing near marginal external cost fixes the peak, and lump-sum returns keep the marginal incentive.
Mileage rebates undo the incentive, and a peak exemption removes the charge where congestion occurs.

items.prompt: A start-up ride-hailing platform must attract both riders and drivers in a new city on limited funds. Riders are very price-sensitive, and each added rider raises driver earnings a lot. Drivers are less price-sensitive and value rider volume highly. Which pricing design is best?

options.label: Charge both sides the same fee so that neither side receives a cross-subsidy from the other
Subsidise drivers heavily and charge riders more, since drivers are the less price-sensitive side
Price each side at its own marginal cost, since pricing above cost on either side deters usage
Waive or subsidise rider fees to build rider volume, and recover costs through a commission on drivers who value access to riders

rubric: In two-sided markets, subsidise the price-sensitive side that creates the most cross-side value and charge the side that gains.
Equal or cost-based fees ignore cross-side externalities, and charging riders more would stall growth.
